rv.q: There are some big themes covered in this musical – war, love and artistic recognition – and it is a credit to Owen that they are handled with confidence and at times with great skill.
Like Monet's, this musical's ambition sometimes comes at a cost, but it still lands in a place of beauty and deep feeling.

Suffice to say, whilst everyone involved with A Mirrored Monet has committed wholeheartedly to its success, the scenes they are attempting to lift from the book feel rather dry and akin to a well-researched biographical lecture rather than a heartfelt piece of entertainment a la La Boheme.

Sure, there’s something a bit fun about seeing that Monet and Renoir were great friends, struggling in obscurity together, while their mentor Manet was only just about breaking through the snobbery of the stale art world. But besides some name-dropping and the usual creative struggles, there isn’t much to tell here.

cn.t: This ambitious Monet musical earns mixed-to-negative reviews for its well-intentioned exploration of the artist's life and the women around him, but critics question whether the subject matter works as musical theatre.
